goshs WebDAV --no-delete bypass: DELETE blocked (403) then MOVE succeeds (2xx) on same path AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core CVE-2026-64863 exploit signature on WebDAV/HTTP logs: a client's DELETE to a resource is correctly rejected with 403 by --no-delete, then the same client issues a MOVE for the same source path that returns 201/204, deleting or clobbering the file the policy was meant to protect. Correlating the blocked DELETE with the successful MOVE on the same source+path within a short window isolates deliberate bypass probing from benign WebDAV traffic. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit control-flow: DELETE returns 403 while MOVE on the same source path returns 201 (rename) or 204 (Overwrite:T RemoveAll). Same src+URL pairing of a blocked delete and a successful move is the CVE-2026-64863 fingerprint, not a generic WebDAV template. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://api.osv.dev/v1/vulns/GO-2026-4606 • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-64863
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDAV servers (SharePoint, Nextcloud, IIS WebDAV) where a client legitimately DELETEs then MOVEs unrelated files
  • WebDAV-aware clients (Windows Explorer redirector, Cyberduck, Cadaver) that retry a delete as a move-to-trash operation
  • Backup/sync agents that receive 403 on a locked resource then rename it
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) legitimately probing WebDAV verbs during an authorized scan
  • Web app that returns 403 for DELETE by policy but permits MOVE for renames as intended design
Suppression filter
// Scope to hosts you know run goshs (WebDAV file drop), e.g. filter DstHostname/dest to the artifact-server inventory, and require the DELETE and MOVE to share the SAME SrcIpAddr and Url before alerting.
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the destination host is a goshs instance (banner `goshs/vX`) started with `--no-delete`/`-w`; pull the full request pair for src IP + URL and check whether the MOVE 204 carried `Overwrite: T`. 2) CONTAIN: Stop/patch the goshs service (upgrade to v2.1.4+ where MOVE is delete-gated) or restrict the WebDAV port to trusted IPs; snapshot the served directory before further loss. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all MOVE 2xx from the same src IP across the served tree, check filesystem delete/rename events by the goshs process, and review other goshs advisories (CVE-2026-50138 read-only/upload-only bypass) on the same host.
let Window = 60s;
let Blocked = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "DELETE" and HttpStatusCode == "403"
| project BlockTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, Url, DstHostname;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "MOVE" and HttpStatusCode in ("201","204")
| join kind=inner Blocked on SrcIpAddr, Url, DstHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (BlockTime .. BlockTime + Window)
| project TimeGenerated, BlockTime, SrcIpAddr, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs process deletes or renames files despite --no-delete (CVE-2026-64863 impact) AIActions on Objectives High
Confirms real data loss from the WebDAV MOVE bypass by hunting file deletion/rename events whose initiating process is goshs while its command line carries --no-delete. Because --no-delete is supposed to make goshs never remove files, any FileDeleted/FileRenamed originated by that process under that flag is the bypass executing (rename removes the source; Overwrite:T triggers RemoveAll on the destination). Rationale: Pins to two article facts: the initiating binary is `goshs`, and its `--no-delete` command line is what the deletion is supposed to be impossible under — so goshs itself performing FileDeleted/FileRenamed is direct impact confirmation of the MOVE bypass rather than a generic file-deletion query. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://api.osv.dev/v1/vulns/GO-2026-4606
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • goshs run WITHOUT --no-delete where deletion/rename is expected behaviour (filter requires --no-delete so this is largely excluded)
  • Authorized red-team using goshs as a legitimate file-drop and cleaning up its own artifacts
  • Operator manually restarting goshs and clearing the served directory
  • A differently-named binary containing the substring 'goshs' in an unrelated toolchain
  • Antivirus quarantining a file inside the goshs-served path (initiating process would be the AV, not goshs)
Suppression filter
// Already tight: the --no-delete requirement excludes normal goshs deletion. To further reduce noise, restrict FolderPath/TargetFilePath to the goshs served directory (the value passed to `-d`).
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the goshs command line to confirm `--no-delete`/`-w`, and list the deleted/renamed file paths and their prior contents from backups or file-audit history. 2) CONTAIN: Kill the goshs process and upgrade to v2.1.4+ (MOVE now delete-gated); restore any destroyed artifacts from snapshot; restrict the WebDAV port. 3) HUNT: Correlate each deletion timestamp with the WebDAV MOVE 2xx access-log entry (UC1) to identify the source IP, then sweep for the same actor touching other goshs hosts or exploiting sibling goshs CVEs (CVE-2026-50138).
DeviceFileEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "goshs"
| where ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, PreviousFolderPath, PreviousFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "goshs"
| where EventType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable goshs deployment: WebDAV file-server started with --no-delete (CVE-2026-64863 exposure) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces hosts running a goshs instance launched with the --no-delete protection flag (and WebDAV enabled), which on goshs <= v2.1.3 / <= v1.1.4 is silently bypassable via MOVE. This is a pre-exploitation exposure hunt so defenders can patch to v2.1.4+ or firewall the WebDAV port before the DELETE/MOVE bypass is abused. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact vulnerable invocation (`goshs -w --no-delete -d ...` / `--webdav --no-delete`) and affected versions (<= 2.1.3 / <= 1.1.4). Finds the exploitable configuration itself, giving defenders a patch-before-abuse window rather than waiting for the MOVE to fire. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-64863
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration tests / red-team engagements legitimately standing up goshs for file transfer
  • Security lab / training environments running goshs intentionally
  • Instances already upgraded to v2.1.4+ where the flag combination is present but the bug is patched (validate version from banner)
  • Internal-only goshs on an isolated segment where the WebDAV port is unreachable by untrusted clients
  • A wrapper script or alias named 'goshs' unrelated to the file server
Suppression filter
// Reduce authorized-usage noise by excluding known pentest jump hosts: | where DeviceName !in~ ("redteam-01","pentest-lab-01")  — populate with your sanctioned goshs operator hosts.
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the goshs version (banner `goshs/vX.Y.Z` or package metadata) and whether the WebDAV port is exposed to untrusted networks. 2) CONTAIN: If <= v2.1.3 (or v1 <= 1.1.4), upgrade to v2.1.4+ where MOVE is gated by --no-delete, or firewall the WebDAV listener to trusted IPs only. 3) HUNT: For any exposed vulnerable host, pivot to UC1 (DELETE-403/MOVE-2xx web-log correlation) and UC2 (goshs file deletion) to determine whether the bypass was already exercised, and inventory other goshs hosts org-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--webdav","-w")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "goshs"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--webdav","-w")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs SFTP server started with empty-credential basic auth (CVE-2026-62325) AIExploitation High
Hunts for the goshs binary launched with -sftp and a -b basic-auth value that has an empty password (e.g. -b 'admin:') and no -fkf key file. That exact combination leaves both PasswordHandler and PublicKeyHandler nil, causing gliderlabs/ssh to set NoClientAuth=true and accept unauthenticated SFTP sessions. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable invocation shape: goshs binary + -sftp + a -b value ending in a colon (empty password) + absence of -fkf. The empty-password regex `[^\s:']+:` anchored to a token boundary avoids matching legitimate user:pass configs, so this fires only on the CVE-2026-62325 condition. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/patrickhener/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-62325/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-40884/ • https://github.com/patrickhener/goshs/commit/0e715b94e10c3d1aa552276000f15f104dee2f32
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentester intentionally standing up an open SFTP drop with -b 'admin:'
  • CTF/lab infrastructure running goshs with empty password on purpose
  • Automation script that templates a placeholder credential (user:) before injecting the real password
  • Internal ad-hoc file share where the operator relies on network ACLs instead of auth
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pentest", "redteam", "lab-") or DeviceName startswith "CTF-")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the goshs process is still running and identify the SFTP listen port from the command line; check whether the host is internet-facing (DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing / public IP). 2) Contain: kill the goshs process and block inbound to its SFTP port at the host firewall; if data exposure is possible, snapshot the served directory before termination. 3) Hunt: pivot to inbound connections to that port from external IPs and to goshs file read/write events (UC4/UC5) to determine whether an unauthenticated client actually connected and transferred files; upgrade goshs to v2.1.4+.

| where ProcessCommandLine has "-sftp"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+'?[^\s:']+:'?(\s|$)"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

goshs -b flag with empty username or password segment AIExploitation Medium
Complementary hunt that parses the goshs -b basic-auth argument and surfaces any invocation where either the username (`:pass`, CVE-2026-40884) or the password (`user:`, CVE-2026-62325) segment is empty, excluding the -fkf mitigation. Extracts and projects the parsed values so the analyst sees the actual credential shape without hand-editing. Rationale: Parses the -b argument the article calls out (`admin:` empty password, `:pass` empty username) and filters on an empty segment rather than a fixed string, catching both CVE variants and any future malformed input while excluding the -fkf fix. Projecting BAUser/BAPass means the query runs as-is and shows the analyst the exact credential shape. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/patrickhener/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-62325/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/patrickhener/goshs/GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator intentionally disabling password (empty password) for a quick internal transfer
  • Config templating leaving `user:` placeholder before the secret is filled
  • goshs used without -sftp (HTTP-only) where empty basic-auth is a different, lower-impact exposure
  • Automated deployment scripts that pass credentials via env var and leave the -b arg half-populated
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName startswith "CTF-" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pentest", "redteam"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the projected BAUser/BAPass to confirm which segment is empty and whether -sftp is also present (SFTP path is the critical one). 2) Contain: if -sftp and empty password, terminate the process and restrict the listener; if HTTP-only, assess data sensitivity before acting. 3) Hunt: search the same host for inbound external connections to the goshs port and for goshs-initiated file writes to confirm exploitation, then patch to v2.1.4+.

Unauthenticated SFTP file operations by goshs following inbound connection AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates an inbound connection accepted by the goshs process with subsequent file create/modify/delete activity initiated by that same goshs process within a short window. This surfaces the read/write/delete file access the advisory attributes to the auth bypass, distinguishing an actively-used SFTP server from an idle one. Rationale: The advisory states the bypass grants read/write/delete/rename file access over SFTP. Tying goshs-process file operations to an inbound accepted connection (the SFTP session) within 5 minutes is the closest endpoint-observable proxy for actual unauthenticated file transfer, and is far higher-fidelity than goshs file activity alone. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/patrickhener/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-62325/
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate authenticated goshs SFTP session (with proper -fkf or full credentials) doing normal transfers
  • goshs used as an intended internal file share where uploads are expected
  • Backup or sync job connecting to an authorized goshs instance
  • Analyst/admin testing the server from a jump host
Suppression filter
| where not (ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP) and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-fkf")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the joined RemoteIP/SrcIpAddr — is it external or an unexpected internal host? Check the goshs command line for -fkf and the credential shape (correlate with UC1/UC2). 2) Contain: if the session is unauthenticated (empty-password config) and the source is untrusted, kill goshs, block the source IP, and preserve the served directory. 3) Hunt: enumerate every file TargetFilePath touched during the session window for data staged/exfiltrated, and check for follow-on execution of any written payload.

goshs SFTP listener accepting external inbound connections AIDelivery Medium
Flags inbound TCP connections to the goshs SFTP listener ports (2121/2222 per the PoC) originating from non-RFC1918 sources, or accepted by the goshs process itself at the EDR layer. Exposure of a goshs SFTP listener to external clients is the wire-side indicator of the auth-bypass being reachable/exploited. Rationale: The PoC connects to goshs SFTP on port 2121; goshs is an ephemeral operator tool never meant to be internet-facing, so an externally-sourced inbound connection to its listener (or one accepted by the goshs process) is a strong exposure/exploitation signal for the unauthenticated bypass. Private-range sources are excluded to focus on external reachability. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/patrickhener/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-62325/ • https://github.com/patrickhener/goshs/commit/0e715b94e10c3d1aa552276000f15f104dee2f32
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned external file exchange deliberately hosted on goshs (with proper auth)
  • Internet-wide scanners (Shodan/Censys) touching the exposed port
  • Penetration test or bug-bounty researcher connecting from an external IP
  • NAT/proxy that makes an internal client appear as a public source IP
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-fkf")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the goshs listener is genuinely internet-facing and identify the source IPs and whether the process was started with the empty-password config (correlate UC1). 2) Contain: remove the external exposure (firewall/security-group rule), and if the config is vulnerable, stop goshs and rotate any data exposed. 3) Hunt: pull the file operations tied to those sessions (UC4) to gauge data access, geolocate/enrich the external source IPs against threat intel, and confirm remediation to v2.1.4+.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^goshs(\.exe)?$"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize ConnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 10), Sources = make_set(RemoteIP, 50) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber in (2121, 2222)
| where NetworkDirection == "Inbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))
| summarize ConnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Sources = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 50) by DvcHostname, DstPortNumber
| order by FirstSeen desc

Endpoint traffic to cubepilot.org during 24 Jul 2026 DNS-hijack / AiTM window AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunt for any host that resolved or connected to cubepilot.org or its subdomains (portal, discuss/forum, docs) during the 24 July 2026 DNS-hijack window, when traffic was redirected to attacker infrastructure holding fraudulent TLS certs. Any credentials entered on those services may have been captured. Surfaces the resolved RemoteIP so an analyst can identify the attacker-controlled address. Rationale: Anchors on the exact victim domain (cubepilot.org and subdomains portal/discuss/docs confirmed on CubePilot's own security notice) bounded to the 24 Jul 2026 hijack window; make_set on RemoteIP/DnsResponseName surfaces the attacker-controlled resolution so no attacker IP needs to be hardcoded. Cross-checked against: • https://cubepilot.com/security-notice/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cubepilot-drone-software-dev-hit-by-dns-hijacking-to-intercept-traffic/
ATT&CKT1557 T1584.002 T1056.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineer legitimately browsing docs.cubepilot.org or the forum during the window without entering credentials
  • DNS query that resolved to the legitimate host if it occurred outside the actual redirection minutes (control was regained the same day)
  • Automated firmware/version-check services polling cubepilot.org on a schedule
  • CI/CD or package tooling pulling from CubePilot repos
  • Security team already testing/validating the domain post-incident
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ResolvedIPs for each hit; any answer outside CubePilot's normal hosting ASN during 24 Jul is the attacker endpoint — pivot all hosts sharing that IP. 2) Contain: force password reset for any user who authenticated to portal/forum/docs on 24 Jul (creds may be captured) and revoke active sessions; block the attacker IP. 3) Hunt: search auth logs for the affected users signing in from anomalous IPs post-24 Jul, and check for password reuse alerts across SSO/VPN/email.

| order by FirstSeen asc

| order by FirstSeen asc

CubePilot firmware/file downloaded from cubepilot.org on 24-25 Jul 2026 (possible tampered supply chain) AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunt for firmware images or any file downloaded from cubepilot.org on 24-25 July 2026 — the window CubePilot flagged as unverified pending checksum review. Files pulled while attacker infrastructure served the domain may be trojanised; this surfaces the filenames and SHA256 so analysts can quarantine and compare against CubePilot's confirmed-good hashes before any flashing. Rationale: Keys on FileOriginUrl containing cubepilot.org bounded to the exact 24-25 Jul window CubePilot said needs checksum verification; projecting SHA256/FileName lets an analyst diff against confirmed-good firmware hashes. Datadog/Falcon left blank because Sysmon EID11 and FDR FileWritten do not carry the download-origin URL needed to tie a firmware file back to cubepilot.org. Cross-checked against: • https://cubepilot.com/security-notice/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cubepilot-drone-software-dev-hit-by-dns-hijacking-to-intercept-traffic/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1584.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Firmware download later confirmed clean once CubePilot publishes verified checksums
  • Documentation/PDF or non-firmware asset pulled from cubepilot.org (not a flashable image)
  • Re-download of a pre-24 Jul firmware that a developer already had
  • File served from a CDN/mirror rather than the hijacked origin
  • Automated build agent caching CubePilot artifacts
Suppression filter
| where FileName has_any (".apj",".px4",".bin",".hex",".elf")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list distinct SHA256 + FileName from the hits; compare each hash against CubePilot's confirmed-good firmware manifest — any hash not on the allow-list is suspect. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block flashing on affected engineering hosts, and isolate any UAV/bench system that was already flashed from a 24-25 Jul image pending inspection. 3) Hunt: on hosts that downloaded a suspect image, look for the flashing tool executing (ground-station/uploader), unexpected child processes, and outbound connections from the file's downloading process to non-CubePilot IPs.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,

DeviceProcessEvents

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)

| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

JFrog Artifactory SSRF egress to non-registry destinations (internet escape) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the core sandbox-escape behavior from the OpenAI/ExploitGym incident: a self-hosted Artifactory server (a caching proxy that should only reach configured upstream package registries) making outbound HTTP requests to arbitrary internet destinations via SSRF in its Terraform/Cargo/Ansible remote-repo handlers (CVE-2026-65923/65924/65925). Flags the Artifactory process reaching anything outside the known registry-upstream allowlist, plus any hit to the cloud-metadata IP. Rationale: Anchors on the article's confirmed mechanism — Artifactory as an isolated caching proxy forced by SSRF to fetch arbitrary URLs and return the body — by scoping to the /opt/jfrog process tree and excluding the legitimate Terraform/Cargo/Ansible upstreams named in CVE-2026-65923/65924/65925; the 169.254.169.254 clause catches the classic SSRF metadata pivot. Cross-checked BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, and CVE aggregators. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-models-used-artifactory-zero-days-to-escape-to-the-internet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/jfrog-confirms-openai-models-exploited.html • https://app.opencve.io/cve/?product=artifactory&vendor=jfrog
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Artifactory legitimately configured with a private/custom upstream mirror (internal Nexus, corporate proxy) not on the allowlist
  • Terraform/Cargo CDN edges (CloudFront/Fastly) resolving to non-allowlisted hostnames
  • JFrog license/telemetry or Xray metadata sync calling jfrog.io / jfrog.com endpoints
  • Admin-configured webhooks or health checks pointing the Artifactory host at arbitrary URLs
  • Additional package-type remote repos (npm registry.npmjs.org, PyPI, Docker Hub) enabled on the same host
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("cloudfront.net","fastly.net","jfrog.io","jfrog.com","npmjs.org","pypi.org","docker.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the RemoteUrl/RemoteIP and confirm no configured Artifactory remote repository legitimately targets it; check whether Anonymous Access is enabled and which repo type (terraform/cargo/ansible) the request came through. 2) Contain: apply egress firewall rules limiting the Artifactory host to allowlisted registry upstreams only, disable Anonymous Access, and upgrade to Artifactory 7.161.15 Self-Managed. 3) Hunt: pull the Artifactory request.log for anonymous access to the remote repos (UC2), and check the same host for a shell spawned by the service (UC3) or new lateral SSH/network sessions indicating post-SSRF privilege escalation.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/opt/jfrog", "artifactory")
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254"
   or (RemoteIPType == "Public" and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
       and not(RemoteUrl has_any ("registry.terraform.io","releases.hashicorp.com","static.crates.io","index.crates.io","crates.io","galaxy.ansible.com","github.com","githubusercontent.com")))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SourceHostName has_any ("artifactory", "jfrog")
| where ApplicationProtocol in~ ("http", "https", "ssl")
| where isnotempty(DestinationHostName)
| where not(DestinationHostName has_any ("registry.terraform.io","releases.hashicorp.com","static.crates.io","index.crates.io","crates.io","galaxy.ansible.com","github.com","githubusercontent.com"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort) by SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Artifactory Server SSRF Outbound to Cloud Metadata Endpoint
id: 8b3f1a2e-6c47-4d9a-9e11-2f0d7c5b4a90
description: JFrog Artifactory service process connecting to the 169.254.169.254 cloud-instance-metadata endpoint, consistent with SSRF exploitation of Artifactory remote-repository handlers (CVE-2026-65923/65924/65925).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-models-used-artifactory-zero-days-to-escape-to-the-internet/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/jfrog-confirms-openai-models-exploited.html

    DestinationIp: '169.254.169.254'
  condition: selection
level: high
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName=/(jfrog|artifactory)/i

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK

Anonymous access to Artifactory Terraform/Cargo/Ansible remote repositories AIDelivery Low
Hunts the exploited precondition of the Artifactory zero-day chain: requests to the Terraform, Cargo, or Ansible remote-repository endpoints performed by the built-in anonymous principal, which is the state (Anonymous Access enabled) required to reach CVE-2026-65923/65924/65925 without credentials. Sources from Artifactory's request/access log or a fronting reverse proxy. Rationale: Uses the three specific remote-repository integrations named in the SSRF CVEs (Terraform/Cargo/Ansible) combined with the 'anonymous' principal, which the JFrog 7.161.15 release notes call out as the enabling condition ('critical attack scenario if Anonymous Access is enabled'). Telemetry is app-log dependent, hence Low confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-models-used-artifactory-zero-days-to-escape-to-the-internet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/jfrog-confirms-openai-models-exploited.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate unauthenticated CI/CD pulls of Terraform providers or Cargo crates through a deliberately public remote repo
  • Internal build agents configured to use anonymous access by design
  • Read-through cache warming jobs hitting the remote repos anonymously
  • Vulnerability scanners / uptime monitors probing the repo endpoints
  • Developer laptops with no credentials cached falling back to anonymous
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Anonymous Access is intentionally enabled on these remote repos; review the source IPs and volume — internal CI ranges are expected, external or single-host bursts are not. 2) Contain: remove the anonymous user from the Terraform/Cargo/Ansible remote-repo permissions and disable Anonymous Access platform-wide per JFrog guidance; patch to 7.161.15. 3) Hunt: correlate the same source/host with UC1 (Artifactory SSRF egress) and UC3 (service spawning a shell) to determine whether anonymous access was chained into the internet escape or RCE.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName in~ ("artifactory", "java", "tomcat") or SyslogMessage has "artifactory"
| where SyslogMessage has "anonymous"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("terraform", "cargo", "ansible")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("GET", "HEAD", "PUT", "POST")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog anonymous (terraform OR cargo OR ansible) (GET OR HEAD OR PUT OR POST)
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/terraform/*" OR Web.url="*/api/terraform/*" OR Web.url="*/cargo/*" OR Web.url="*/api/cargo/*" OR Web.url="*/ansible/*" OR Web.url="*/api/ansible/*") AND Web.user="anonymous" by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.http_method Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/terraform/*" OR Web.url="*/api/terraform/*" OR Web.url="*/cargo/*" OR Web.url="*/api/cargo/*" OR Web.url="*/ansible/*" OR Web.url="*/api/ansible/*") AND Web.user="anonymous" by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.http_method Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
JFrog Artifactory service process spawning a shell or network tool (RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-65617 (remote code execution on an Artifactory package-service container): the Artifactory/JFrog service tree (Java/Tomcat under /opt/jfrog) spawning an interactive shell or download/network utility — the canonical post-exploitation signature of RCE against the Artifactory app. This is the execution step the models used to escalate after SSRF. Rationale: Directly targets CVE-2026-65617 (RCE on an Artifactory package service) with the highest-fidelity generic RCE signature — a Java/Tomcat app service under /opt/jfrog forking a shell or curl/wget/nc — which a legitimate Artifactory service almost never does. Named process-tree parent makes it alerting-tier. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-models-used-artifactory-zero-days-to-escape-to-the-internet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/jfrog-confirms-openai-models-exploited.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Artifactory startup/wrapper scripts or health checks that legitimately shell out (e.g. system.yaml bootstrap, DB migration)
  • Admin running maintenance commands inside the Artifactory container/service context
  • JFrog installer/upgrade routines invoking curl/wget to pull packages
  • Backup or log-rotation jobs launched under the service account
  • Container entrypoint scripts spawning sh during restart
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("installer", "upgrade", "migrate", "health", "bootstrap", "logrotate", "backup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and the grandparent chain — startup/upgrade scripts are benign, but reverse-shell strings (nc -e, bash -i, python -c socket) or curl to an external IP are true positives. 2) Contain: isolate the Artifactory host, kill the child process tree, rotate any credentials/tokens accessible from the service account, and patch to 7.161.15. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for UC1 SSRF egress and UC2 anonymous repo access to reconstruct the SSRF→RCE→escape chain, and review outbound SSH/lateral connections for the privilege-escalation/lateral-movement stage described by OpenAI.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/opt/jfrog", "artifactory")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","python","python3","perl","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility in~ ("authpriv", "auth", "daemon", "user")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/opt/jfrog", "artifactory")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/bin/sh", "/bin/bash", "/bin/dash", " python", "curl ", "wget ", "/bin/nc", "socat")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)

| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vBulletin fixes critical pre-auth RCE flaw with public exploit

BleepingComputer
2026-07-28 3 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

A critical vulnerability in the vBulletin forum software allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary PHP code through template rendering. [...]

CVEsCVE-2026-61511
ATT&CKT1190

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] vBulletin CVE-2026-61511 pre-auth RCE via ajax/render/pagenav template request
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] vBulletin web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx) spawning OS shell after CVE-2026-61511
vBulletin CVE-2026-61511 pre-auth RCE via ajax/render/pagenav template request AIExploitation High
Hunts direct HTTP requests to the vBulletin 'ajax/render/pagenav' render endpoint carrying a malformed 'pagenav[pagenumber]' value — the exact route/parameter Egidio Romano's PoC abuses to reach runMaths()->eval(). Legitimate clients never POST this template route directly, so a crafted hit is a high-fidelity exploitation attempt against an unpatched (<=5.7.5 / <=6.2.1) instance. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC route 'ajax/render/pagenav' and the 'pagenav[pagenumber]' parameter named in the SSD advisory and article, plus a phpfuck-style special-char burst (^()!~) that the regex-bypass payload requires. Direct external requests to this internal render template are not legitimate user traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://ssd-disclosure.com/vbulletin-runtime-template-runmaths-preauth-rce/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/public-exploit-released-for-patched.html • https://securityonline.info/vbulletin-preauth-rce-cve-2026-61511/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vbulletin-flaw-execute-php-code/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Acunetix) probing the CVE-2026-61511 endpoint
  • Internal red-team / pentest validating the patch level
  • Security researchers or bug-bounty testers hitting a staging forum
  • WAF-in-monitor-mode replaying blocked payloads into access logs
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors misconfigured to request raw ajax/render paths
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Acunetix", "masscan", "zgrab") or DeviceAction in ("blocked", "denied", "deny"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the target host's vBulletin version (banner / footer / admincp) is <=5.7.5 or <=6.2.1 and check the HTTP status returned — a 200 to a POSTed pagenav render with a non-numeric pagenumber implies successful reach into runMaths(). Pull the full request body from the WAF/proxy. 2) Contain: Block the source IP at the WAF, virtual-patch the ajax/render/pagenav route, and expedite upgrade to 6.2.2 or Patch Level 1 (6.2.1/6.2.0/6.1.6); 5.x has no fix so isolate/decommission. 3) Hunt: Pivot to UC2 on the web host for php-fpm/apache spawning shells within seconds of the request, and review outbound connections from the web-server account for reverse shells or tool download.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "ajax/render/pagenav"
| where RequestMethod == "POST" or RequestURL has "pagenav[pagenumber]" or RequestURL matches regex @"[\^\(\)!~]{4,}"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vBulletin web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx) spawning OS shell after CVE-2026-61511 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation stage of CVE-2026-61511: the vBulletin PHP runtime executing arbitrary system() commands via eval(), which surfaces as php-fpm/php/httpd/apache2/nginx spawning a shell or recon/download binary under the web-server account. This is the RCE actually landing, independent of whether the exploit request was logged. Rationale: Chains directly off the article's mechanism: runMaths() feeds attacker input to PHP eval(), and the public PoC calls system() for an interactive shell under the web-server account — so php-fpm/apache/nginx as parent of sh/curl/whoami is the RCE landing. Parent-child pairing (not bare shell) keeps fidelity high. Cross-checked against: • https://ssd-disclosure.com/vbulletin-runtime-template-runmaths-preauth-rce/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/public-exploit-released-for-patched.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vbulletin-flaw-execute-php-code/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • vBulletin/CI cron jobs where PHP legitimately shells out (image processing via ImageMagick 'convert', 'sendmail' mail delivery)
  • Backup/maintenance scripts run under www-data invoking tar/curl
  • Plugin functionality that calls exec() for thumbnails or media transcoding (ffmpeg)
  • Composer/deploy automation running as the web user
  • Monitoring agents launched under the web-server service account
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ImageMagick", "convert ", "ffmpeg", "sendmail", "/usr/sbin/") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "cron")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — phpfuck RCE typically yields short recon (id/whoami/uname) or a download (curl/wget to an external IP). Correlate the process time with a UC1 ajax/render/pagenav request from the same host within ~60s. 2) Contain: Isolate the web host, kill the offending php-fpm worker and child, rotate any DB/API creds readable by the web account, and block observed egress IPs. 3) Hunt: Search for dropped webshells under the vBulletin docroot (FileWritten of .php by the web user), new cron entries/service units for persistence, and lateral SSH/DB auth from the compromised host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","whoami","id","uname","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php-cgi","/php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","whoami","/id","uname","curl","wget","python","perl","/nc","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anomalous Host header on Poweradmin OIDC/SAML/logout endpoints (CVE-2026-54588) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-54588 exploitation: requests to Poweradmin's /oidc/callback, SAML ACS/SLO, or /logout endpoints carrying an HTTP Host header value that has never been seen for that site in the 30-day baseline. Poweradmin embeds HTTP_HOST verbatim into the redirect_uri/ACS URL sent to the IdP, so an attacker-controlled Host value is the exploitation primitive. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable endpoints (/oidc/callback, SAML ACS/SLO, LogoutController) and the root-cause primitive (untrusted HTTP_HOST embedded in callback URLs). Baseline anti-join surfaces the attacker's poisoned Host (e.g. attacker.com) without hardcoding the victim's legit hostname. Cross-checked GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx and SentinelOne/NVD (CWE-20/601, CVSS 9.6). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-54588/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54588
ATT&CKT1190 T1656
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new vhost/hostname added to the Poweradmin front-end (rename, new DNS name, migration)
  • Uptime/health-check probes (Pingdom, StatusCake) that send synthetic Host headers
  • Load-balancer or Kubernetes ingress health probes hitting endpoints with pod-IP Host values
  • Vulnerability scanners run by the org's own security team (Nessus/Burp) sending crafted Host headers
  • CDN/WAF origin pulls that rewrite the Host to an internal origin name
Suppression filter
| where CsHost !in~ ("localhost","127.0.0.1") and CsHost !endswith ".internal" and CsHost !endswith ".svc.cluster.local" and not (CsUserAgent has_any ("Pingdom","StatusCake","kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests to the anomalous CsHost on the auth endpoints; confirm the Host value is not an owned domain and check whether the request produced a 301/302 to an IdP authorize URL (redirect_uri would contain the attacker host). 2) Contain: set interface.base_url in Poweradmin config/settings.php (activates the safe branch immediately) and upgrade to 4.2.4/4.3.3; fix the reverse proxy so it does not pass proxy_set_header Host $http_host. 3) Hunt: check the IdP for AADSTS50011 redirect_uri-mismatch events and any successful admin sign-ins in the hour that followed; audit PowerDNS zones (MX, SPF/DKIM, CAA, delegation) for unauthorized changes.

let AuthPaths = dynamic(["/oidc/","/saml","/logout"]);
let Baseline = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(LookbackDays) .. ago(RecentHours))
    | where CsUriStem has_any (AuthPaths)
    | summarize by CsHost;

| where TimeGenerated > ago(RecentHours)
| where CsUriStem has_any (AuthPaths)
| where isnotempty(CsHost)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on CsHost
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Requests=count(), SampleUri=any(CsUriStem), SrcIPs=make_set(CIp,20), Statuses=make_set(ScStatus,10) by CsHost
| order by FirstSeen desc

Host header fuzzing burst against Poweradmin auth endpoints from single source AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects unauthenticated reconnaissance/injection probing for CVE-2026-54588: a single source IP hitting Poweradmin OIDC/SAML/logout endpoints with 2+ distinct HTTP Host header values inside a 10-minute window. This is the shape of an attacker enumerating which flow reflects HTTP_HOST into the outbound redirect_uri. Rationale: Self-contained fan-out on the article's specific auth endpoints; multiple distinct Host headers from one IP is the unambiguous signature of host-header injection probing described in the advisory (unauthenticated, no credentials required). No allowlist/placeholder needed. Thresholds (2 hosts, 3 requests) are conservative and self-evident from the attack shape. Spike of AADSTS50011 redirect_uri mismatch at IdP (poisoned Poweradmin callback) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the IdP-side footprint of CVE-2026-54588 when the OIDC/SAML IdP is Entra ID: a burst of AADSTS50011 (redirect_uri / reply-URL mismatch) failures on a single application within an hour. Entra rejects the attacker-poisoned redirect_uri (attacker.com/oidc/callback) because it is not a registered reply URL, so a cluster of 50011 on the Poweradmin app is high-fidelity evidence of active redirect_uri poisoning. Rationale: Directly maps the article's exploitation mechanic (poisoned redirect_uri sent to the IdP) to the IdP error it produces. Corroborated by Microsoft Learn / SSOJet: AADSTS50011 'spiking on URIs you never deployed' is the documented signature of an attacker probing crafted redirect_uri values — exactly this CVE. 5/hr threshold separates probing from a single stray config typo. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-code-aadsts50011-redirect-uri-mismatch • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx
ATT&CKT1528 T1190
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine app-registration reply-URL misconfiguration after a Poweradmin upgrade or hostname change
  • A single trailing-slash / http-vs-https typo in the app's configured base_url producing repeated 50011 for legit users
  • Developer/staging instance of Poweradmin pointed at the production app registration
  • Reply-URL propagation lag (~60s) right after an admin edits the app registration
  • Load-balanced deployment where one node has a stale/incorrect base_url
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIPs has_any ("10.","192.168.") and Users == 1)
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the failing redirect_uri/reply-URL values in the sign-in detail — legit misconfig repeats one owned URL, an attack shows external/attacker hostnames or many distinct URIs. 2) Contain: if attacker hosts are present, treat affected users as at-risk (revoke sessions/refresh tokens for any who authenticated), lock the app to strict reply-URL matching, and force Poweradmin's interface.base_url + patch. 3) Hunt: pivot to successful sign-ins for the same users from new IPs in the following hour (see companion UC), and audit PowerDNS zones for MX/SPF/DKIM/CAA tampering.
AADSignInEventsBeta

| summarize AttemptCount=count(), Users=dcount(AccountUpn), UserList=make_set(AccountUpn,20), SrcIPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by Application, ApplicationId, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where AttemptCount >= 5   // 5+ reply-URL mismatches/hr on one app = probing, not a one-off config typo
| order by AttemptCount desc

Victim account takeover: new-IP sign-in within 1h of redirect_uri mismatch (CVE-2026-54588) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates the two halves of a successful CVE-2026-54588 account takeover on Entra: a successful sign-in for a user from an IP absent from their 90-day baseline, occurring within one hour of an AADSTS50011 redirect_uri-mismatch event for that same user. Catches the case where the attacker captured the victim's authorization code via a poisoned redirect_uri and then used it/logged in. Rationale: Implements reviewer suggestion #1 and ties the article's stated outcome ('IdP redirects the victim's authorization code to an attacker' → full account takeover, no credentials) to observable telemetry: a fresh-IP success closely following a 50011 for the same user. Baseline anti-join + 1h temporal window is high-fidelity and article-specific to the redirect-poisoning flow. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-code-aadsts50011-redirect-uri-mismatch
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User travels / switches to a new mobile-carrier or home IP the same hour a legit 50011 config error fired
  • VPN or corporate-proxy egress-IP rotation introducing a 'new' IP for an existing user
  • New device enrollment where the user re-auths from an unfamiliar network after an app-registration reply-URL fix
  • Roaming user behind CGNAT whose apparent IP changes between the failure and the success
  • Admin testing the app registration (deliberately triggering 50011) then logging in from a lab network
Suppression filter
| where DelayMin <= 60 and NewIP !startswith "10." and NewIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the success IP's geo/ASN vs the user's baseline and whether the 50011 FailIP differs; check what the session did next (consent grants, PowerDNS zone edits, mail-flow rules). 2) Contain: revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens, force password reset + re-MFA, and block the new IP; if the user is a Poweradmin admin, freeze PowerDNS zone changes. 3) Hunt: review PowerDNS for MX hijack, SPF/DKIM additions, CAA removals and subdomain delegation; sweep other users for the same 50011→new-IP pattern and confirm the app is patched (4.2.4/4.3.3) with interface.base_url set.
let Lookback = 7d;
let WindowHours = 1h;
let BaselineDays = 90d;
let UserIpBaseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(Lookback))
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | summarize by AccountUpn, IPAddress;
let RedirectFailures = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where ErrorCode == 50011
    | project FailTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, FailIP = IPAddress, Application;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| join kind=leftanti UserIpBaseline on AccountUpn, IPAddress
| join kind=inner RedirectFailures on AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (FailTime .. FailTime + WindowHours)
| project SuccessTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, NewIP = IPAddress, Country, Application, FailTime, FailIP, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, FailTime)
| order by SuccessTime desc

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 11 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new Mirai-derived botnet called Tengu can use a compromised Linux device's hardware watchdog to trigger a reboot when defenders kill its main process. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Tengu ELF-header corruption ('ELFOOD') of Linux reboot/shutdown utilities · [LLM] Tengu guardian process masquerading as kernel thread [kworker/0:0] · [LLM] Tengu immutable-binary persistence via chattr +i on Linux/IoT
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Tengu botnet C2 / IPFS beacon to 64.89.163.8 on TCP 9931 and 8080 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Telnet credential brute force against internet-exposed IoT/Linux devices (Tengu dropper entry) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts high-volume inbound Telnet (TCP/23) connection attempts from a single external source against Linux/IoT hosts, the entry vector Nozomi observed for the Tengu dropper on its honeypots. Article-specific because Tengu spreads exclusively via Telnet default/weak-credential brute force rather than an exploit. Rationale: Uses the article's stated entry vector (Telnet TCP/23 credential brute force on internet-exposed IoT/Linux) as a volumetric single-source pivot; port 23 to public-facing embedded hosts is inherently high-signal since legitimate Telnet exposure is rare. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html
ATT&CKT1110 T1078.001 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal network/security scanner (Shodan-style, Nessus, Nmap) sweeping TCP/23 across the estate
  • A misconfigured legacy management tool that legitimately polls Telnet on embedded gear
  • ISP/upstream background internet scanning noise hitting an exposed device
  • Load-balancer or NAT health checks probing port 23
  • Penetration-test engagement against IoT segment
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<known_scanner_ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target hosts are IoT/embedded and that TCP/23 is genuinely internet-reachable; check whether any attempt succeeded (post-auth session, new process). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter, disable/firewall Telnet on the exposed devices, and rotate any default credentials. 3) Hunt: on any device that accepted a session, pivot to Tengu post-compromise indicators — outbound TCP/9931 to 64.89.163.8, a process masquerading as [kworker/0:0], chattr +i on new binaries, and modified /sbin/reboot|shutdown utilities.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where LocalPort == 23 and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Attempts = count(), Devices = dcount(DeviceId), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP
| where Attempts > 20   // empirical Telnet brute-force volume threshold from a single source
| order by Attempts desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort == 23
| summarize Attempts = count(), Denied = countif(DeviceAction in~ ("deny","drop","blocked","reset")), Targets = dcount(DestinationIP), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP
| where Attempts > 20   // brute-force volume threshold on Telnet/23 from a single source
| order by Attempts desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as attempts, dc(All_Traffic.dest) as targets, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=23 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.action | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where attempts>20 | sort - attempts
| tstats summariesonly=false count as attempts, dc(All_Traffic.dest) as targets, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=23 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.action | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where attempts>20 | sort - attempts
Tengu botnet C2 / IPFS beacon to 64.89.163.8 on TCP 9931 and 8080 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any egress from an internal host to the hardcoded Tengu C2 IP 64.89.163.8 over TCP/9931 (plaintext registration/heartbeat) or TCP/8080 (IPFS gateway payload retrieval). Article-specific because both the IP and the two ports are named in the analyzed sample's configuration. Rationale: The C2 IP 64.89.163.8 and both ports (9931 for plaintext registration/heartbeat, 8080 for the IPFS gateway) are explicit strings from the analyzed sample; a hardcoded single-IP + non-standard-port pair is near-zero-FP. URLhaus independently logged 17 malicious Mirai-related URLs at the same IP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html • https://urlhaus.abuse.ch/host/64.89.163.8/
ATT&CKT1571 T1071.001 T1105 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate IPFS node/user on the estate happening to reach port 8080 on that host (unlikely — IP is a known-bad C2)
  • Threat-intel or sandbox detonation VM deliberately beaconing to the IOC during analysis
  • Security researcher/blue-team validating the IOC from a lab host
  • Stale NAT/proxy log attributing the connection to the wrong internal source
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal source device and the initiating process (Defender InitiatingProcessFileName / Falcon ContextImageFileName); confirm the host is IoT/Linux. 2) Contain: block 64.89.163.8 at the perimeter, isolate the device from the network, and preserve volatile state before power actions (Tengu corrupts reboot/shutdown binaries). 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts beaconing to the same IP/ports, and on the infected host review systemd units, /etc/init.d, /etc/rc.local, shell rc files, cron, and /dev/watchdog before reimaging.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "64.89.163.8"
| where RemotePort in (9931, 8080)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "64.89.163.8"
| where DestinationPort in (9931, 8080)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHost = SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Tengu ELF-header corruption ('ELFOOD') of Linux reboot/shutdown utilities AIInstallation Medium
Hunts non-package-manager modification of the on-disk reboot/shutdown/halt/poweroff binaries, which Tengu overwrites (ELF magic replaced with 'ELFOOD') to block defenders from cleanly restarting or powering down a compromised device. Article-specific: standard admin/patch flows never rewrite these binaries outside the package manager. Rationale: Directly targets Tengu's named self-defense behaviour (overwriting reboot/shutdown ELF headers with 'ELFOOD'); modification of these system binaries outside a package manager is a rare, high-fidelity signal on Linux/IoT. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html
ATT&CKT1222.002 T1562.001 T1529
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OS upgrade replacing coreutils/systemd/busybox binaries (should show a package-manager initiating process)
  • A vendor firmware-update agent rewriting /sbin binaries in place
  • Admin manually recompiling/replacing a shutdown wrapper
  • Configuration-management tool (Ansible/Puppet copy module) deploying a patched binary
Suppression filter
// Defender: already excludes package managers via InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (...). Add vendor firmware agent if known:
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("fwupd","swupdate")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the initiating process and confirm it is NOT a package manager; on the host, check whether the reboot/shutdown binaries' ELF magic has been replaced with 'ELFOOD' (first bytes not \x7fELF). 2) Contain: isolate the device and DO NOT trust local reboot/shutdown commands — use an out-of-band power/PDU action; snapshot for forensics first. 3) Hunt: correlate with a [kworker/0:0] masquerade process, /dev/watchdog usage, chattr +i on new binaries, and beacons to 64.89.163.8:9931 on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/sbin/reboot","/sbin/shutdown","/sbin/halt","/sbin/poweroff","/usr/sbin/reboot","/usr/sbin/shutdown","/usr/sbin/halt","/usr/sbin/poweroff")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","yum","dnf","opkg","busybox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/sbin/reboot","/sbin/shutdown","/sbin/halt","/sbin/poweroff","/usr/sbin/reboot","/usr/sbin/shutdown","/usr/sbin/halt","/usr/sbin/poweroff")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("dpkg","apt","rpm","yum","dnf","opkg","busybox"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, DvcAction, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Tengu ELFOOD Corruption of Reboot/Shutdown Utilities
id: c4a7d9e1-3b62-4f80-9d15-8e0a2c6b41f7
description: Detects modification of Linux reboot/shutdown/halt/poweroff binaries by a process that is not a package manager, matching Tengu's ELF-header corruption to block defender recovery commands.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/28
tags:
  - attack.t1222.002
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.t1529
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename:
      - '/sbin/reboot'
      - '/sbin/shutdown'
      - '/sbin/halt'
      - '/sbin/poweroff'
      - '/usr/sbin/reboot'
      - '/usr/sbin/shutdown'
